To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) mutations in the GCase-encoding GBA1 gene cause widespread lysosomal depletion in GD neurons; (2) this is due to defective clearance of autophagic vesicles; (3) the TFEB-mediated lysosome biogenesis program is down-regulated in GD neurons; and (4) the lysosomal depletion in mutant cells is reversed by treatment with recombinant glucocerebroidase, and this effect is enhanced in the presence overexpressed TFET.

(i) GBA1 mutations in iPSC-derived neurons (iPSC-neurons) cause widespread lysosomal depletion and a block in the autophagic flux; (ii) TFEB expression, stability, and lysosomal protein biosynthetic capacity are reduced in mutant iPSC-neurons; and (iii) rGCase reverses the lysosomal depletion in GD iPSC-neurons, and this action is enhanced by overexpressing TFEB.

The main takeaway from our work is that

GBA1 gene mutations interfere with TFIB-mediated lysosomal biogeneration, and that the lysosomal alterations described in the paper are likely to be major contributors to the neurodegeneration seen in GBA1-related diseases.

GCase is required for maintaining lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in neurons, and that the loss of GCase activity leads to a block in lysosomal biogenesis due to reduced TFEB expression and activity.

GBA1-associated lysosomal dysfunction in GD neurons involves a block in autolysosome formation due to reduced lysosomal numbers, and that TFEB plays a key role in maintaining lysosomal numbers and autophagy in neurons.
